review:
I first played the original PC version of FF7, and then later the PlayStation version.

After purchasing and replaying the Steam version, I can wholly recommend it as the definitive version of Final Fantasy VII to play. I'll start off with some quick points about this version in comparison to previous versions. The actual game will be discussed in more detail below.

Vs Playstation:
+Smoother look on the characters
+No disc swapping
+English translation has been tidied up and the plot is more coherent (No one seems to talk about this, but it's major in my eyes)
-Swearwords have been replaced with !@#$ style characters.

Vs original PC release:
+Hassle-free, in my experience (40+ hours) <-- This is the key thing for me.
+PSX music added, as opposed to the awful original PC music. Huge plus! The song "One Winged Angel" now has vocals like it should do :)
+Rendered characters are now synced perfectly when walking over a pre-rendered video.
+Videos look smoother and match the PSX version, which is very nice in comparison to original release.
-Default keyboard controls need two hands. Original PC release had default keys all on the Numpad. Meaning you can scratch your chin or drink coffee while playing. Easily resolved anyway :)
-Yet another thing you have to create an account for. This time for Square Enix. Once you've done so, you can pretty much forget about it.

I have an Xbox controller, but never tried it admittedly, so can't comment on that! I found the game plays perfectly with keyboard.

It's surprising how well Final Fantasy VII has aged. I hadn't played the game for nearly 7 years now, and was expecting it to be incredibly ugly. Don't get me wrong, it IS incredibly ugly, albeit in a charming way now. Rather than a good looking game being badly ported, this is a bad looking game that's been ported just right. You can't change your resolution (to my knowledge), but there's absolutely no need to. The game makes use of pre-rendered backgrounds and the resolution they chose for the 3D characters was a good compromise between smoothness and not sticking out too much from the backgrounds. It does look much better than the PSX version, and a bit better than the original PC release.

I am also happy that they stuck with the original PC version's English translation. If you've only ever played FF7 on one platform before, you may not know that the PC version had a much neater, tidier translation. I'm not talking about a complete overhaul like some of the other Final Fantasy remakes. This is still the original story told in what the original PSX translation was trying to do. Any line that was fine before, is unchanged. They simply removed some (admittedly funny) spelling mistakes, and only changed lines that really did not make any sense at all. It makes the game feel more natural and therefore I highly recommend a replay if you've only played on the PSX before. The one noticeable, and unfortunate, change is that the swearing has been replaced with !@#£ style symbols. You can still tell they're swearing and what word they were going to say, but this unnecessary censorship felt a bit out of place. Still, it doesn't make or break the game. And just to be clear, this isn't new to the Steam version as it was present on the original PC release.

Also, as I might as well say it now: The story IS really good. As FF7 is one of the most popular entries in the franchise, it sometimes gets a lot of flak from people who seem to only want to dislike popular things. These are personal games, which you should play for yourself, and FF7 offers a deceptively complex story, with a fantastic combination of twists. 'Twist' is a harsh word, because it implies a sudden and unexpected change in the story's direction. This is not the case. The 'twists' are completely natural and only serve to make everything before fit into place better. The combination I mentioned earlier is in reference to twists which you will definitely understand on your first time through, and some which may only make sense with a bit of thinking or a replay. The latter are not essential to understand, but you'll feel a satisfying sense of revelation if you do. All in all, this is a well-thought out constructed tale. It may not be as fast-paced as you'd like, but the end result is very satisfactory.

The gameplay itself is surprisingly fast for a 90s JRPG. You can get through battles pretty quickly, and most of the attack animations are short enough to not be too annoying. With the exception of summons; huge magical attacks shown in a lengthy animation of a monster being summoned and inflicting damage on your enemies.

The Materia system is still great and offers lots of customisation for your characters, although it's not as complex nowadays as it used to be. To be clear, Materia are 'gems' which you attach to characters to give them extra abilities or magic. As a Materia is used, it gains its own experience and gets progressively more powerful. The only complexity comes from managing who has what materia, and this is the one area of the game where the age really shows. You can only quick swap between character's Materia screens for the three characters in your party, rather than every available character. Therefore you are forced to constantly swap characters in and out to get the best setup. [EDIT: A number of comments have corrected me and pointed me to the Exchange option, which negates this complaint of mine!]

Is it worth £10? Admittedly, this port probably generated no where near the amount of work needed to justify the price, but the quality of the game does. Therefore it's a tough question to answer. I suppose if you look at what you're getting, then yes, it is worth the price. Your first time through the game can literally take 60-70 hours. My replay was 40 hours long, and I know the game extremely well.

This is now my favorite way to play Final Fantasy VII. And that is probably the one thing you needed to know.

EDIT: Voted this game for "Villain most in need of a hug" award ;)

I can't really recommend this version of the game to most users, for three primary reasons:

1) DRM. The game will not start the first time until you set up a Square-Enix account and log into it, and if Square's servers are having problems, you simply will not be able to play the game you just bought, as happened to me when I last reinstalled it and was locked out of the game for a full day. This is a game from 1998 with essentially no online features, there is no reason online connectivity should be required to play it, it's easy for pirates to circumvent and is only hurting the experience of legitimate users like myself. Square, stop it.

2) The controller support is broken. The launcher that lets you map buttons to a controller cannot correctly map to several of the buttons on standard PC controllers like the Xbox One, DS4, etc. The game is technically completable without those buttons but you lose functionality with the world map camera and in some of the minigames and you lose the option to switch between stick and D-pad which I do a lot in this game. If you want to play the game with full controller functionality you have to use third party software to remap the buttons to keyboard inputs. That's ridiculous.

3) My biggest complaint is that despite multiple updates, this game out of the box still has the same broken framerates as the 1998 PC port this is based on. Battles, including the battle menu, are locked to 15fps. This not only makes them very choppy and unresponsive compared to the PSX version, it also breaks certain functionality with the controls. Field screens do not have locked framerates at all and will run with a 10-15% speedup depending on your hardware, completely throwing off the expertly directed cinematic pacing of the game (which in its original version was locked at 30fps for those screens).

So if your plan was to just purchase the game and play through it as is with no modifications, I would say zero stars, do not buy, this is a broken product and you will not be able to play the game as intended by the developers.

With that said, problems two and three are fixable. There is third party controller to keyboard mapping software, it works well. There are mods to fix the framerate issues, the 60fps battles mod and the frame-rate limiter mod are both good and with both installed you will have 99% the same experience as the PSX version. Both of these mods can be found in the package "The Reunion" and are pretty easy to install and uninstall, so if you want this version to be playable, you can make it that way.

And the good news is, once the game is restored to its intended state, it's fantastic, it's a five star game and everyone should play it. So I can tentatively recommend it to people who are willing to do some digging around online to figure out how to fix all of these problems, but be aware that you're paying for a broken piece of software and there's no guarantee that later updates might not break mod compatibility and cause these issues to come up again. If that sounds like more than you want to commit to, try to track down the PSX disc version instead.

Final Fantasy VII is a classic, there's no debating that. With it's first release on the Playstation back in 1997, this release is a repackaged version of the PC port released in 1998.  With cloud saves and achievements, it doesn't really stand out to people who may have already bought the game or have it elsewhere.

Final Fantasy VII uses almost all the assets from the original PC version of the game. Music was re-encoded to OGG Vorbis, but was still based off of fairly ugly MIDI tracks that the PC used. Thankfully they are easy to replace as some poeple have even decided to use remixes of said tracks instead.

Visually the game is very dated. 2D backgrounds, 3D sprites from that era with resolution stretching 2D elements while providing a modicum amount of improvement to the 3D models. While in the field, higher resolutions don't really help, but in battle scenes and in full 3D environments (Chocobo Racing, Submarine Minigame), there is a noticeable improvement.

Controls are a bit awkward as for a 360 controller, the triggers, d-pad, and right stick aren't usable. However, you can get around that either by binding everything to usable controls or using a utility like JoytoKey.

This is a bare-bones re-release, with the hard work for making it work with a modern OS stripped away for most people.

Update: SquareEnix has managed to replace the MIDI quality music with PSX quality tracks. This means the game's music sounds extremely detailed compared to the original PC release.

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]
If you scroll down the (serious) positive reviews for this game, you no doubt see many people expressing their nostalgic love for this legendary piece of their childhood. I stand among these people. For many of us who were kids in the 90s, [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] was and always will be the first truly [i]epic[/i] game we ever played. So I’ll admit that I am definitely biased to love it, as it was my personal favorite game during a number of years of my childhood. But that isn’t why I’m going to recommend that you consider trying it. You should consider it because [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] is a classic piece of video-game history that revolutionized the genre and because it’s a kickass game. 

At the time it first released, there were a handful of other large RPGs with huge worlds and a lot of gameplay (relative to the era), but they were uncommon and unpopular in the Western world. [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] reached a pinnacle of awesomeness for RPGs that was unprecedented and subsequently elevated the genre into the mainstream gaming market outside of Japan. Not only did it have sound RPG fundamentals, but the sheer amount of variety of gameplay it offered was quite revolutionary for the genre. Chocobo racing and breeding, the motorbike scene, the snowboard scene, the Golden Saucer, the Don Corneo segment, and more all contributed to shattering the status quo for the genre. A lot of young gamers went from not knowing about RPGs to one of them being their favorite game ever. Not only that, but it became one of the cornerstones which provided a foundation for the genre to grow towards what it has become today. If there was a Video Game Hall of Fame, [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] would no doubt be in it. 

Obviously, with more recent RPG blockbusters from franchises like [i]The Elder Scrolls[/i], [i]The Witcher[/i], and [i]Fallout[/i], it is hard to continue to consider [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] to be an “epic” game by today’s standards. Somehow it still feels that way to me. Or at the very least: since I enjoy the genre, I still find it quite fun to play.

So I will admit that it definitely has been a long time since [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] was one of the best games in existence. That said, even after the erosion of the sands of time, the game still feels exciting, intriguing, and massive to me. Even on my 8th playthrough I pick up on new subtleties in the story or discover new secrets and items. 

The story is interesting, if not a bit convoluted. (Some of the story was cut away to make it “less confusing for the Western market” or some such silliness. This wound up making it more confusing.) The Materia system is fun and, combined with the traditional XP leveling, continuously offers the satisfaction of progress as you play through the campaign. The world is intriguing and still semi-large(ish) even by modern standards. The characters are perfect clichés of the very clichés that they themselves introduced. And one of the best parts of the game will always be the intimidating boss battles with the signature music. It is doubtful there will ever be another kid who says [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] is his favorite game ever, but most modern fans of the genre will enjoy this game despite its age.

So there are a few reasons you may want to consider trying this game if you never have.

If you consider yourself a true aficionado of the gaming industry, you will probably want to play [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] at least once in your life. Even though there is a “remake” on the way (or out by the time you read this), I would argue you should play this version at least once to really experience a legendary piece of video game history in this semi-unadulterated state.

Or: if you don’t care about any of the historical mumbo-jumbo, and just are looking for a fun, turn-based JRPG, then you can comfortably look to [b]Final Fantasy 7[/b] for that as well.

Parents and grandparents went halfsies on a PSX and FFVII for Christmas '97 or '98 (can't remember), and they even got me an ASCII second controller. But none of us knew a memory card was also required. So I replayed the first hours of the game over and over for a week until I had bugged my dad enough to fork the cash out for one (he was pretty thrifty and initially I almost shat my pants when I saw that they had ACTUALLY even got a console for me). And as I got older, I started analyzing things more and I see why my young mind was so enthusiastic about this game, and made inferences about why my older mind would've never like this game if I was 39 in 1997.

[h1] Steam Deck/Controller Configuration Tips! [/h1]
The default button mapping is all messed up in this PC port, so for full enjoyment here's what to do:

If playing directly on the Deck, open FFVII to the "PLAY" screen. Tap "SETTINGS" on the touch screen, then go to the JOYSTICK tab. Tap on each input option and press the corresponding button on your Deck to map the controller properly.

[b]DO NOT modify the controller configurations inside the game itself (via the party menu where you see your characters faces and the menu options)![/b]

Not only will it not fix anything, you could further screw up the controls and make the game literally unplayable.

[h1] My recommendations for Steam Deck button mappings:[/h1]

OK = A
CANCEL = B
MENU = Y
UP = Stick Up
LEFT = Stick Left
RIGHT = Stick Right
DOWN = Stick Down
START = "Hamburger" Button
SWITCH = X
PAGE UP = L1
PAGE DOWN = R1
TARGET = R3 (Right Stick In)
ASSIST = "Two Window" Button
CAMERA = L3 (Left Stick In)

This will get you pretty close to the original PS1 control scheme, though you could swap the OK and CANCEL mappings if you'd like (some online walkthroughs use this layout). Same mapping logic works for XBox controllers.

Don't forget that STEAM + X brings up the onscreen keyboard, which you will need to use to start the game. When it boots up, open the keyboard and input the X key (not the X button). This will bring you to file select, where you can play "normally" with a controller.

-------

With that out of the way, I'll just say this port obviously has issues. The default controller mapping is already bad enough, but also the in-game button icons are their nonsensical designations (PAGE UP, SWITCH, ASSIST, etc) instead of "A" or "B". Thus you really need to understand which designation belongs to which controller button or else you'll have a bad time. And I do recommend playing on a controller over KB&M.

But beyond that, I had no performance issues and was able to play as much as four hours straight on a single battery charge.

Final Fantasy VII was the first game I played on the original PlayStation, and no other game had ever impressed me on that level before. It was a complete eye-opener and remains, for me, one of the most important JRPGs ever made.

Even small things felt monumental at the time. The multiple discs alone made the game feel huge. Then came Midgar, dark, industrial, and oppressive, only for the world to suddenly open up after the first chapter into a vast, freely explorable overworld. The sheer sense of scale was overwhelming. Secrets, optional content, hidden locations, side stories. Everything felt magical and full of discovery.

The turn-based combat system was fantastic, but what truly set it apart was the Materia system. Experimenting with different combinations, building characters in flexible ways, and discovering powerful synergies felt endlessly rewarding. It was deep without being inaccessible, and it encouraged creativity rather than rigid class roles.

And then there is the story. Epic, emotional, and unforgettable. The characters are wonderfully written and still iconic to this day. Cloud, Tifa, Barret, Aerith, Sephiroth. They are more than just party members; they feel like companions on a long and often painful journey. The death of Aerith, even today, remains one of the most shocking moments I have ever experienced in a game. Back then, it left me staring at the screen in complete silence. I had never seen a game do something like that before.

Final Fantasy VII also taught me what grinding really meant. Standing in front of the final boss and realizing I simply could not win was a completely new experience. Going back, leveling up, preparing properly, and finally overcoming that challenge felt incredibly satisfying.

Years later, I replayed the game on PC. The higher resolution and improved textures make it easier on modern eyes, but I deliberately avoided mods. This is a game whose original experience should remain untouched. Its flaws are part of its identity.

Final Fantasy VII is pure magic. A timeless milestone, a genre-defining masterpiece, and for me personally, an unforgettable experience that shaped how I see games to this day.

Final Fantasy VII isn't a game that will blow anyone away with its dialogue. There's goofiness right around the corner from serious moments. Its models are blocky, dated, and odd. It's a bit convoluted at times. The world is obtuse. 
And yet, despite all this, the game is incredible. 

If you've never played a Final Fantasy game, this is perhaps the one to start with. Yes, there is the Remake trilogy, but if you can stomach old games and their sensibilities at least a little bit, I would very much recommend this one. 
To say it was a leap from VI is an understatement. VI on the SNES was already pushing boundaries with its storytelling and character work, for VII to take that into a 3D environment (using the PS1's tech), nail down most of what made VI work and then expand upon it was nothing short of incredible. 
Final Fantasy VII only really excels against present day games in one department. The music. The soundtrack is perhaps my favourite in gaming, certainly at least in the top 5. What makes the game special is that nearly everything else is done extremely competently. 
The gameplay loop won't blow people away, but it is addicting and diverse. The characters are close to a level of nuance, but the game balances its large and varied cast (even the optional party members) in a way that makes it seem effortless.
The world is built in a linear fashion — you start out in the most detailed city in the game — but the narrative enhances the story that's filled with great mysteries. And yes, the answers are satisfying. 

I mentioned the game was goofy before in a negative light, perhaps that was a bit harsh. The goofiness in a lot of these places make its world feel endearing. The casual dialogue with people on the streets is memorable. The light-heartedness mostly serves to have those darker portions hit hard, and hit hard they do.
It's all the little things that make the game. The way the handholds shake on the train. The vistas that they didn't have to go as hard as they did for. The wacky enemies. The many minigames. It all adds up to something that surpasses its contemporaries, and hell even a lot of games that come out today. I've rarely been as immersed in a world as I was traipsing through Midgar's lively neon-lit slums, under the giant steel plates of the higher class folk and that great central tower looming over all. 

On a technical stand point, I would actually recommend using mods. A few of them really take away the dated aspects of the game. I initially played it in 2014 with no mods, and then again during the Pandemic on my PS4. This time, I used the 7th Heaven mod manager (which compared to other games was a cakewalk to use) and it was the best experience I've had with the game yet. 
Turning the game widescreen, upscaling the backgrounds that were already pretty great, getting a more accurate translation (still without Japanese honorifics, I'm not that much of a weeb), and allowing a speed-up option really enhanced the experience, while still exploring the core of a game the developers designed. I highly, highly recommend adding just a few mods. You don't have to feel bad; they ended up doing models that actually look close to human in FF VIII so it's nice to change it here a few years before the devs did.

With Rebirth coming out on PC, and the third game on the horizon, I can only recommend people give this a go. The Remake is fun, but it does some of my favourite moments a bit worse (and some better, to be fair). Older games can be fun, especially because they trusted the player's imagination more. If you need an adventure, this one is waiting for you.

Disc 1 was probably the slowest of the discs (at times), but disc 2 really picks up the pace of story development that builds up to the final dungeon and boss in disc 3.

Gameplay wise, FF7 is quite dated now, and there is not too much that you can do if you are used to great QOL new gen games. For its time, FF7 gameplay was incredible with the freedom and depth of things to do and explore. However in 2025, although the system is very much still playable, the game didn't age the best coming from the early polygon era. The good part is that it uses an ATB (which is quasi turn based) instead of a straight action based combat system, which at least makes combat still fun (this is the same system that the later pixel FF games used prior to FF7). I would consider the gameplay passable, but not a selling point for the game anymore.

Overall, FF7 is a great game to experience. Although dated now, there is still a lot of fun to be had in the game. I recommend people give this a shot (if they are willing to overlook graphics) to get the best experience for subsequent FF7 games (including Remake).

For a long time I refused to believe that there were people out there who didn't know about Final Fantasy 7. But lo and behold, they exist. I've met them. This is for you, who heard about the game but ended up finding the trailer unappealing and the graphics trashy.

FF7 was almost released as a SNES game but ended up in the PS, with the questionable glory of 3D graphics with pre-rendered 640x480 backgrounds. Sounds like old stuff, 'cause it is 22 years old; things were not as shiny and texture rich back then as they are now, and that's why developers had to do some magic to keep you immersed and even sympathise with your extremely-polygonal-main-character-who-is-not-even-voice-acted.

FF7 defined a new era for RPGs. It was first games of the series to break away from their usual fantastic glamourous scenario with knights and wizards in favour of a a Steampunk Fantasy in an environment which did not hit far from home. The main plot of the game is still unsurprisingly relevant even today: a critique against companies exploring the resources of the planet, risking to cause irreversible damage in the name of profit. And while a large portion of the story happens in the gray slums of Midgar, you'll witness a very familiar world once you visit Kalm, Nibelheim or Rocket City. The music is the very definition of a masterpiece for videogames; look for FF7 orchestra in youtube and relax... and the plot?

The combat system was extremly exciting for those days, but most people now would be craving for blood and action. You won't find that in FF7, which is more intelligence-driven: you can defeat the strongest bosses without touching the controller if you plan ahead! There are thousands of minigames spread throughout the game too, some of which are quite fun.

FF7 inspired also myriad of spin offs (e.g. Dirge of Cerberus, Crisis Core and Advent Child) and even some fan-made remakes of the first few minutes of the game with modern graphics - you don't find that kind of love easily. 

If you absolutely need modern graphics to be able to enjoy a game, however, good news for you. This masterpiece is being remade, and the combat system will also be modernized. I wouldn't suggest you to wait, but to buy this, play now, buy the new release, and then play the new release. And then play this again. There are few titles which will ever be worthy to be mentioned alongside FF7 in terms of pure geniality.

A classic from the Playstation 1 era. This is one of the first RPG games I ever played and has always set the standard of what I expect from an RPG. It features turn based, but active combat, a fun and more-or-less easy to follow story, and decent characters and personalities though some border on the cliche. Finaly Fantasy 7 has a good amount of side quests and minigames that can eat up plenty of time. From snowboarding to breeding and racing chocobos the handful of side quests and metagames can keep you entertained for quite a while. 

               I found that, as with almost all RPGs I play, one of my favorite things to do is collect all the strongest magics and weapons. There are monsters you can encounter that are even stronger than the last boss at the end of the main story. On top of that there are magic abilities that, if you have the patience to level them up, can make the final boss a walk in the park. Getting these weapons and magics require a great deal of grinding though, which is someting I find to be rather offputting. Squeezing every last ounce of gameplay from this title will probably take you somewhere in the neighborhood of 70 hours if youre the occational gamer like me. 

             Since it's initial release the game has not really aged well. If youre looking for a top-notch Final Fantsy expierience I would point you to one of the newer titles. It's kind of hard to look at the old graphics in high resolution. To help this they have an "original graphics" mode for people like me. It keeps the display to 480x640, but without the inherit funnyness of a SDtv set you still see plenty of jaggies and protruding polygons. The graphics didnt stop me from playing through one of my old favorites though. 

             Another gripe I have about the age is the clunky controls when roaming about but it's nothing you cant get used to. The button layout can be a tad confusing on the keyboard. If you happen to have a gamepad it eases this considerably, but you're probably going to have to spend a moment remapping the default controls-- no biggie.  

          One of my favorite aspects about the steam version is the cloud saving. True: its usless if you dont have an internet connection where you want to play. But I like the ability to play on my PC, go wherever, and pick the game right back up on my laptop. Aside from that there is also a "character booster" if you get stuck...or want to be a badass. I have not used the feature mainly because I forgot my square-enix login stuff moments after i made it. 

              Its not particularly weak in any areas but isnt as deep in character skill devlopment as I would like sometimes. Rather than molding your character(s) into what you want them to be, you have to play to each character's strengths-- again, no biggie. 

              Theres no voiceover, which is a huge plus for me. The story is good, characters are likeable, the gameplay is solid, and its good on length. It's probably 20 hours on the game clock on a casual playthough if you ignore endgame badass equipment, skills, and sidequests. All-in-all its worth it if it's on sale, but if you just want a stroll down memory lane you might be better off digging out the old PS1.

[b]TLDR:[/b] It adds nice QoL stuff, but it’s built on pre-release source code, has small but noticeable differences from the PS1 version. ALSO requires a Square-Enix account to open the game. Mods can fix most issues, but you shouldn’t need them.

[b]=============================[/b]

I’m giving it a recommend only because I love Final Fantasy VII and the game itself is amazing, but I’m not a huge fan of this port.

Game-wise, it's phenomenal. The mechanics, the world-building, the soundtrack, the everything, it's all tops in this game. It's [b]not[/b] a perfect game, definitely has some flaws, but it's a damn good one. Some people love FFVII, some loathe it. Biggest criticism I have is that the story does slow and meander a lot after you get to the world map (trying not to spoil anything), but it's still great. I think it's one of the best OG Final Fantasy games.

To give this port some credit where it's due: the translation was tightened up a [i]little[/i] bit, it supports modern resolutions in widescreen (16:9), ultra-wide (21:9), and super-ultra-wide (32:9), has autosaves, reworked menus, allows for both keyboard and controller, and some lite QoL enhancements. Works on the Steam Deck great as well. They also, for whatever reason, re-added mouths on most models, which was left unused on the PS1. I like it, gives a little more personality. Not sure why they did this, though? Possibly because of something I talk about later...

As for why I don't like this port that much? Well, first, I don't understand what in gods name possessed Square-Enix to require an account login to open the game. That is pretty much my biggest reason for not wanting to recommend.

Second, this was infamously built off pre-release source code since the final build's code was lost. Back then, Square didn't keep project files after games were completed (??? I'd love an explanation on why they did this). Because of this, it results in some very minor differences between this PC port and the final PS1 release. They’re not big, but you do notice them if you’ve already played the PS1 version. Small things, like different music playing, things timed EVER so slightly different, and so on.[spoiler]For example, there's a [u]mid-boss fight[/u] on an elevator earlier in the game. In the PS1 version it plays the proper 'Fight On' mid-boss track, which makes sense, right? Well, in this version it just plays the standard battle theme. There's several of instances like this, so it just makes this port [i]feel[/i] wrong or incomplete.[/spoiler]I personally prefer the PS1 version, as these differences are enough to really bug me. It is nit-picky of me, though, as most won't care or even notice at all. Worth mentioning, this can [i]mostly[/i] be remedied by modding the game via [b]7th Heaven[/b], but honestly, meh.

None of this is to necessarily say you shouldn't get this, but beware of what you're buying before you do.

[i]Final Fantasy VII[/i] is a game with such influence and legacy that I don’t feel like I need to explain what it is. As of January 2023, the game has sold [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Fantasy_VII#Sales]over 14.1 million units across all platforms[/url] (!), [url=https://www.metacritic.com/game/playstation/final-fantasy-vii]received high praise[/url] and [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_of_Final_Fantasy_VII]received numerous spin-offs[/url] under the “Compilation of Final Fantasy VII” brand - from a CGI movie sequel to games (even a [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Fantasy_VII:_The_First_Soldier]F2P Battle Royale one[/url]!) to books. One might cynically say that publisher Square Enix is still heavily benefiting from milking the [i]Final Fantasy VII[/i] name but on the other hand, there does seem to be an audience for this cross-media universe – otherwise it wouldn’t have lasted for so long.

Which begs the question, especially with the release of the long-awaited [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1462040/FINAL_FANTASY_VII_REMAKE_INTERGRADE/]Final Fantasy VII Remake[/url]: Is there any reason to still play this version of the original 1997 game? The answer to that question is yes, sorry. There are two simple reasons for that. First, the [i]Final Fantasy VII Remake[/i] is only the first part of a planned trilogy, so playing that would only cover a fraction of the original game. Second, the [i]Final Fantasy VII Remake[/i] is aimed at fans who already played the original game and consequently introduces various story deviations to keep them on their toes. So yes, the Remake doesn’t replace the original [i]Final Fantasy VII[/i] - which leaves us with this 2012 PC port of the game.

First of, let me voice my disappointment here: [i]Final Fantasy VII[/i] received a re-release on PS4, Xbox One, Switch and the Microsoft Windows Store (?!), which is [url=https://finalfantasy.fandom.com/wiki/Final_Fantasy_VII_version_differences#PlayStation_4,_Xbox_One,_Windows_10,_Nintendo_Switch]based on this 2012 PC version sold on Steam[/url]. These re-releases include new features, like a 3x Game Speed Mode, an option to turn battle encounters off as well as a “Battle Enhancement Mode” (max out HP/MP/Limit at the press of a button). I would’ve loved to see these features added to this Steam version as well, considering how they’re especially helping those who just want to experience the best part of [i]Final Fantasy VII[/i] – the story.

Anyhow, as the PC version we’re stuck with on Steam is from 2012, there are thankfully numerous mods out there to improve the experience. I advise checking the [url=https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/Final_Fantasy_VII_(2012)]PCGamingWiki[/url] for more information but I’ll briefly list my recommendations here. First of, there’s [url=https://www.ff7.live/features.html]The Reunion[/url], a mod which offers numerous improvements. Most notably, it offers a relocalization of the game, improving upon the notably bad translation the game got in the West, as well as allowing for 60 FPS during battle scenes (instead of 15 FPS without mods). This mod does disable Steam achievements unfortunately, though you can unlock those manually through the [url=http://www.blackchocobo.com/]Black Chocobo[/url] save editor. Additionally, I installed a mod for [url=https://forums.qhimm.com/index.php?topic=20311.0]upscaled backgrounds[/url], and one for an [url=https://forums.qhimm.com/index.php?topic=20234.msg283477#msg283477]HD UI[/url]. Lastly, I recommend using a program called [url=https://forums.qhimm.com/index.php?topic=14194.0]Ochu[/url], which offers multiple features (like invincibility), though I mainly used it in order to save anywhere in the game, not just at the save points.

To be clear here, these mods can only do so much. [i]Final Fantasy VII[/i] was the first [i]Final Fantasy[/i] to feature 3D graphics instead of 2D pixel art – and while those 1997 PS1 graphics might’ve turned heads back in the day, they’re far from pretty in 2022. Early 3D graphics just didn’t age as well as those SNES sprites, unfortunately. Thankfully, the same can’t be said for the rest of [i]Final Fantasy VII[/i].

Let’s briefly talk about the gameplay first. The “Active Time Battle” system makes a return, though it has received an addition with “Limit” bars – once filled, your characters can unleash an especially powerful attack. Those are nice to look at and a pleasure to unlock, though getting the best limit levels for every character takes way too long. Magic returns in form of “Materia”, which can be equipped in limited slots of weapons and armor.

Personally, I don’t like the Materia system. The benefit here is that powerful spells can easily be swapped to different characters, which is great. My problem here is that each Materia must be levelled in order to make those spells more powerful (Thunder -> Thundara -> Thundaga, for example) and you can’t buy “powered-up” versions in stores. So apart from character levels and limit levels, you might also need to grind Materia in order to succeed in battle. Summons return as well, also in form of (upgradeable) Materia – and [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0t8yQ47qvQI]really sweet cutscenes[/url].

Overall though, the general gameplay works as well as it previously did – though party size went down from four to three characters. There’s an overworld, random encounters, dungeons and bosses. [i]Final Fantasy VII[/i] also introduces several minigames as part of the journey, which are a nice little distraction. Also included is various optional content, however, this unfortunately once again includes entire party characters like in [i]Final Fantasy VI[/i]. I recommend using [url=https://jegged.com/Games/Final-Fantasy-VII/]a guide like this one[/url] to make sure you won’t miss out on them as they’re once again somewhat obtuse to unlock.

I’ll be honest here though, I feel like the star of and the reason for [i]Final Fantasy VII[/i]’s ongoing popularity are the characters and overall story. As the first 3D [i]Final Fantasy[/i], the story presentation here is above and beyond what [i]Final Fantasy VI[/i] could offer with its technical limitations. Now there are long scenes filled with nothing but dialogues and FMV cutscenes, instead of battles every 30 seconds. Characters develop and receive interesting backstories, the villain is almost as well known as the hero today and the world itself full of memorable locations. 

Admittedly though, this isn’t the verdict I reached after my first playthrough on Nintendo Switch. Back then, I was mostly confused about how a story like this would go on to become so popular. I feel like the improved translation of the Reunion mod really did wonders for me here, as my second playthrough allowed me to appreciate its characters and world much more (though the game would’ve benefitted from an epilogue), even though it’s still [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oPE-Ivy9LLg]occasionally goofy[/url] (spoilers!).

In conclusion, [i]Final Fantasy VI[/i] still holds up today – mostly thanks to its story and characters (<3 the Turks). Parts of the gameplay and especially the graphics haven’t aged as well, unfortunately, though there are mods to help with that. For those with little time and/or those not wanting to deal with Materia frustrations, I honestly recommend just playing through the game with “invincibility” enabled through Ochu in order to enjoy the story. I wish the Remake would’ve been more faithful in order to provide the same experience with better gameplay and graphics but alias, this modded PC version of the 1997 original game is the second-best option right now.

New to the Final Fantasy series, I decided to pick this game up after hearing lots of good things about it. Final Fantasy VII is one of those iconic games which you hear so much talk about, that you have to play it in order to see if it matches what people say. And does it live up to expectations? Well, mostly.
[b]Story:[/b]
FF7's story suprised me, as it was quite different to what I had expected, although not in a bad way. From what I'd heard beforehand, I was used to thinking of Final Fantasy 7 as this dark, brooding story set in a dystopian futuristic city, and while this holds true for the first couple of hours, there is so much more to it. As mentioned, FF7 is often seen as quite dark, but in reality it's a game which never takes itself to seriously, and still retains a sense of fun. The story itself is long and developped (it took me around 60 hours to beat the main story alone), and covers several mature themes. I have to say that I found the main story really engrossing, even if I'd heard some spoilers beforehand. If their was one criticism to be had with the story, it's that the latter half of the game doesn't quite manage to meet the standard of the first half, with the plot becoming a bit too convoluted, and difficult to follow.
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay in Final Fantasy VII is good, but nothing spectacular. Being an JRPG, a good deal of gameplay is taken up by turnbased battles. The combat system is simple enough for beginners, but also has enough technique for more experienced players. This makes for several fun battles, although a large number of random encounters, as well as summon attack cutscenes which can take up to two minutes to play out, can make them seem a bit repetitive. I enjoyed the battles for the most part although some of them towards the end of the game, I found very frustrating .As well as battles there are also several minigames such as motorbike chases, or snowboarding which you can try out. These can be fun, but I didn't try them out much. Outside of battles and minigames, you will travel across the world and explore caves, and towns. This is easier said than done, as the static backgrounds can be quite hard to traverse.
[b]Graphics[/b]
It's no secret that Final Fantasy VII's graphics are a bti dated, with some characters looking like lego, but I genuinely didn't mind them that much. They have been sharpened for this release, and some of the battles actually look quite decent. There are several cutscenes as well, which look quite good for the time.
[b]Music[/b]
If there's one thing which is easy to agree on about Final Fantasy VII, it's that it has great music. From killer battle tracks, to heart wrenching leitmotifs, this game has some of the best and most memorable music I've seen in a game. Mr. Uematsu, I salute you.
[b]Verdict[/b]
Final Fantasy VII is an amazing game with a memorable story, some fun battles, and a killer soundtrack. Even the occasional frustrating moment, doesn't stop this from being an incredible game.
10/10

The pace of the game never lets up throughout and is always throwing new and interesting situations, minigames, story beats, enemy types and so much more at you as you progress. There's always a clear direction to move in, with plenty of optional exploration on the way, and always a clear reason to be progressing forwards.
The story and the characters themselves are extremely well presented and not dumbed down at all, they respect your intelligence and I was thankful for that.

Final Fantasy VII: A Landmark in RPG History
Final Fantasy VII, originally released in 1997 for the PlayStation, is often hailed as one of the greatest video games of all time. Its blend of compelling storytelling, memorable characters, and innovative gameplay mechanics set a new standard for the RPG genre.

What Works:
Compelling Storyline:

The narrative follows Cloud Strife, a mercenary who joins a group called Avalanche to fight against the oppressive Shinra Corporation. The story is rich with themes of identity, loss, and environmentalism, featuring numerous twists and emotional moments that resonate with players.
Memorable Characters:

The game introduces a diverse cast, including Tifa, Barret, and Sephiroth, each with unique backstories and development arcs. Sephiroth, in particular, is often regarded as one of the most iconic villains in gaming history.
Innovative Gameplay:

The Active Time Battle (ATB) system introduced a new layer of strategy to combat, allowing players to make decisions in real-time. The Materia system also provided deep customization options for character abilities and spells.
Stunning Visuals and Music:

For its time, the graphics were groundbreaking, featuring beautifully rendered environments and character models. The soundtrack, composed by Nobuo Uematsu, is legendary, with tracks like "One-Winged Angel" becoming instantly recognizable.
Cultural Impact:

Final Fantasy VII played a crucial role in popularizing JRPGs in the West, influencing countless games that followed. Its legacy continues to be felt in modern gaming, with remakes and spin-offs expanding its universe.

What Could Be Improved:

Graphics: While revolutionary at its release, the graphics may feel dated to modern players. The character models and backgrounds lack the detail found in contemporary titles.
Pacing Issues:

Some players may find the pacing uneven, with certain sections dragging on while others feel rushed. The game’s length can also be daunting for newcomers.
Minigames and Side Quests:

While some side quests are engaging, others can feel tedious or less rewarding, which might detract from the overall experience.

Overall Impression:
Final Fantasy VII remains a timeless classic that has left an indelible mark on the RPG genre. Its engaging story, memorable characters, and innovative gameplay mechanics continue to captivate both new players and long-time fans. Whether you're experiencing it for the first time or revisiting it, FFVII offers a rich and rewarding adventure that stands the test of time
A latecomer to the series, but this game is a wonderful journey that truly must be experienced firsthand.

If I had to make a list of the games that most influenced me as a gamer, FF7 would be #1 hands-down. It kick-started my love for JRPGs and to this day is the bar to which I compare every JRPG I play. That being said, I firmly believe that, while FF7 is highly nostalgic for me, it still holds up to this day as an excellent game.

The contemporary setting and aesthetic are highly appealing to me, and strike a nice balance between realism and fantasy. You start in a steampunk-ish modern city called Midgar, with slums that show the town's humble and depressing reality. Yet at the same time, your first two party members are a spiky-haired skinny dude whose sword probably weighs more than he does, and a guy who has a machine gun grafted on his arm.

Despite that, it somehow works and meshes into a cohesive world that pulls you in, with many varied locales and settings. Combined with Nobuo Uematsu's legendary soundtrack, it provides for a truly memorable experience. Seriously, he's the King Midas of video game composers, and FF7 wouldn't be the masterpiece it is without his tracks, some of which would go on to influence video game music as a whole.

The gameplay is top-notch as well, with the materia system providing a nice level of customization and flexibility. Limit breaks, which would become something of a genre standard, basically started here. Back in middle school when I first played FF7, it was like video game crack to me. I would play it on a relative's PSX because I didn't have one at the time, and they had to limit how often I could come over to play it, because otherwise it would be all day, every day.

All that being said, this game has flaws. Being an early 3D game, the character models look like they're made of Legos. The battles have a low framerate by today's standards, and the overall difficulty is pretty easy, even compared to other Final Fantasy games. Yet despite all that, there's something about this game that brings me back to it in a way no JRPG has matched since. I've played through it over a dozen times, installed gameplay mods that up the difficulty, and done various challenge playthroughs to keep the gameplay fresh. That's quite rare considering I'll almost never play a long game more than once or twice.

If you're playing FF7 the first time, play through it with modest expectations, that way the game will likely surprise you instead of possibly disappoint you given its legendary hype and backlash from some people because of that.

In my ongoing and likely futile effort to write a Steam review for every game in my library (#300 out of 612)... it's time for Final Fantasy VII.

As much as I have no business writing a review of Final Fantasy VII, you, too, have no business reading a review of Final Fantasy VII. Why? It should go without saying: it's Final Fantasy VII. It is the [i]definitive[/i] Japanese-style Roleplaying Game. It's the game by which, for better or worse, not just every other Final Fantasy title, but every other JsRPG is judged. It's historical and cultural significance cannot be understated. I'm only here, saying all this, because I'm in the middle of my own Quixotic quest here--[i]what's your excuse?[/i]

I won't bother discussing the narrative (it's great! -- Full of compelling, dynamic characters, unexpected twists, heartbreaking tragedy and heartwarming triumph). I won't bother discussing the presentation (it's great! -- low-poly textureless 3D models are a bit clumsy, but the animation is superb and the 2D backgrounds are exceptionally evocative). I won't bother discussing the music (it's great! -- arguably Uematsu Nobuo's finest work, nearly every track if an absolute classic).

What I will discuss is the more objective merits of the Steam port of Final Fantasy VII: it's a good port, but a far cry from a proper remaster. While the 3D models will look very crisp in high definition, the 2D backgrounds (and FMV cinematics) have not been upscaled at all. I believe there is currently a mod attempting to use AI upscaling techniques to remaster the backgrounds (likewise for Final Fantasy VIII and Final Fantasy IX) but as of this review, it is incomplete. Likewise there are (multiple) mods to replace the original 3D models. Personally I don't see much necessity in replacing the character models, as I think the originals--while very crude--exude a certain degree of charm. The lack of expressiveness, for example, has the unintentional benefit of forcing players to imagine the characters' emotional states based on the literal dialog and present context (and there is an abundance of context! Final Fantasy VII's story is nothing if not emotional). With more expressive characters, as I expect we'll shortly see with the episodic Final Fantasy VII remake project Square-Enix is about to release into the world, I feel the story would lose a lot of its emotional edge--and veer sharply into melodrama.

Which I suppose brings us to the elephant in the room: the upcoming Final Fantasy VII Remake, soon to be released on the Playstation 4, later to be released here on Steam. Statistically, by the time you read this, whoever you are, the remake will already be out there--at least in part--and its very existence will beg the question: why play the original Final Fantasy VII when a newer, sexier version exists?

Because newer doesn't mean better. Because remaking a story very seldom improves a story. Because you'll be paying more for less. Because you'll only get a fraction of the Final Fantasy VII experience and will have to wait years for the next fraction, and years still for the next fraction, and pay up each time. Because Final Fantasy VII is the game beloved by an entire generation of players--multiple generations, if I'm being totally honest--and the remake is not. Because Final Fantasy VII is the genre-defining classic--and the remake is not. Because, because, because: only one of these two titles is, simply, [b]Final Fantasy VII[/b].

Classic. Incomparable. Unforgettable. Timeless.

Note: also played on Sony Playstation.
